rationale: A wins because it keeps its feet on the supplied facts and turns the launch into three usable press lanes without decorating the gaps. Its strongest line, "Whoop's new blood-pressure number isn't a medical reading — and needs a cuff to even start," is sharp, true, and pitchable. B has a smart regulatory angle, but then steps on the rake with "the differentiating claim is blood pressure — a feature nobody has cleared" and "cuff-free blood pressure," neither of which was supplied and one of which clashes with the cuff-calibration fact.
gaps_in_A: "screenless band" is not in the supplied update. It may be true of Whoop generally, but this judging brief does not give you that fact, so it should be framed as proof to verify, not assumed.
"health features are increasingly paywalled" is a broader trend claim that needs evidence beyond this launch. A admits this in proof, but the angle headline still leans on a trend before proving one.
It misses B's best lane: the regulatory split inside one launch, with FDA-cleared ECG beside non-medical blood-pressure wellness insights.
gaps_in_B: "blood pressure — a feature nobody has cleared" is invented. The update says Whoop's feature is not diagnostic; it does not say nobody has cleared any comparable product.
"cuff-free blood pressure" is sloppy against the supplied fact that Whoop requires one-time cuff calibration. That is exactly the kind of phrasing that earns a correction.
"at a company whose entire model is subscription rather than hardware margin" goes beyond the update. The tier gate is supplied; the hardware-margin thesis is not.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is overcomplicated for a launch-led angle set. Unless the user asked for a live news hook, the right move is journalist-fit-check after picking the lane.
